summary: A 1979 description of the universal host table in use at MIT and Stanford, which was meant to be better than the NIC and Tenex host tables. It also describes a compiled binary file for fast lookups.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 752 describes a host table developed at MIT and Stanford. It stores names, addresses, machine details, and nicknames in a text file, with a compiled binary form for faster lookups.

questions: why use a binary host table
what is the universal host table
subtitle: A text host table and compiled lookup format used at MIT and Stanford.

tldr.problem: The NIC host table was sometimes inaccurate, lacked commonly used nicknames and other details, and was awkward for programs to use efficiently.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes text entries for networks and hosts, plus a compiled 36-bit binary file with tables for networks, addresses, sites, and names.
tldr.outcome: The format had been implemented at MIT and Stanford and is presented as a suggested replacement for the host table then in use.

today: RFC 752 describes a host table already implemented at MIT and Stanford and presents it as a suggested replacement for the current host table. The RFC asks for discussion of network naming conventions.

sections.title: Why the Host Table Changed
sections.content:
The authors say the NIC host table was sometimes inaccurate, could omit nicknames used at their sites, and lacked information needed by some programs. Programs also had to be reassembled when the table was included in their source.

The new arrangement uses a source text table and a shared binary file that programs can read after the table changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The local designers needed a host list with more accurate names and details, and a way to update it without rebuilding every program.

sections.title: The Text Host Table
sections.content:
The text file contains NET lines with a network name and decimal network number, and HOST lines with a host name, one or more network addresses, user or server status, operating system, machine type, and optional nicknames.

Comments begin with a semicolon. The RFC describes address formats for ARPANET, CHAOS, and Dialnet entries.
sections.plainLanguage: A network entry names a network and its number. A host entry can list its addresses on several networks, its status, system, machine type, and nicknames.

sections.title: The Compiled Binary File
sections.content:
The binary file is organized into a header and NETWORK, ADDRESS, SITE, and NAMES tables. The tables connect network numbers to addresses, addresses to site records, and names to site records.

The RFC describes the file as a 36-bit data file and uses SIXBIT for stored names. The appendix contains the host table current when the memo was written.
sections.plainLanguage: The compiled file keeps separate lookup tables for networks, addresses, sites, and names. Programs can read the shared file instead of compiling the text list into each program.
